attribution.note: Marcus's own co-authored post, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: Keeps both parts: no particular capability gain over earlier GPT-3, and unprecedented public and press attention. It is a retrospective observation.

contract.note: The plain reading of broad capability across several tasks is fair and ordinary. Narrowing 'unprecedented' to earlier GPT-3 releases is lenient to the speaker but reasonable. No threshold is given for 'particularly'.

evidence.note: A peer-reviewed study of the December 2022 version shows large gains on medical QA over GPT-3 and InstructGPT. That is material counterevidence, but it covers one domain, and the contract says one benchmark cannot settle overall capability.
A contemporaneous report of 1M users in under a week. It shows rapid adoption, but there is no comparable attention series for earlier GPT-3 releases.

reviews.rationale: The packet has one domain-specific comparison showing improvement, which is not enough under the contract to settle overall capability. It also has an adoption report with no comparable baseline. Neither half of the claim is established or refuted on the contract's terms.

semantics.note: Replacing 'predecessors' with 'earlier GPT-3 versions' is a reasonable reading of the context. The 'all the same kinds' quantifier is preserved.

contract.note: Reading the claim as persistence of error categories rather than error rates is fair. Using the families listed in the passage as the scope of 'all' is an ordinary reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch disclosure admits plausible but wrong answers and biased behaviour. It supports persistence of the fabrication and bias families, though it is not independent.
Dated December 2022 logs of the December 15 version show arithmetic mistakes. These are selected demonstrations covering one family.
A predecessor baseline showing untruthful and toxic outputs. It says nothing about ChatGPT itself.

reviews.rationale: The evidence supports persistence of some families (fabrication, bias, arithmetic) and nothing shows any family was absent. Temporal, physical and social reasoning are not covered with matched baselines, so the contract's full support condition is not met.

semantics.note: Keeps 'reliably' and both task families: counting to four, and one-digit arithmetic in simple word problems.

contract.note: Reading the claim as inconsistent success, not total inability, is fair. Assessing the two families separately and adding no numerical cutoff is reasonable.

evidence.note: The error example is dated Jan 24, 2023, after the post, and involves algebra with larger numbers. It cannot speak to either claimed task family in the target period.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence item is outside the target period and covers a different task. The packet has no in-period test records for counting to four or for single-digit word problems, so neither family is settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own co-authored post. The 'in our opinion' label still states the authors' view.

semantics.note: This is a causal-necessity claim tying the errors to a next-word training objective. 'Inevitable' is firm language. 'Engage with meaning' has no operational definition.

contract.note: Reading 'inevitable' as unavoidable is the ordinary reading. Whether the claim can be scored depends on how 'engage with meaning' and causal necessity are interpreted, and the speaker defined neither.

evidence.note: The training description shows SFT and RLHF on top of next-token pretraining. This complicates the premise, but it does not show whether the errors were avoidable.

A Nov 2023 theorem: calibrated models must hallucinate arbitrary facts, but there is no such statistical reason for arithmetic or systematic facts. It partly fits and partly cuts against the claim, and it was not shown to apply to launch-era ChatGPT.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet establishes or refutes that ChatGPT's actual training made the listed error families unavoidable. The theorem covers only some errors and was not shown to apply to this system. The training documentation does not settle avoidability.
